questions.stem: A value function scores each project as the sum over measures of w x m / R. A new feed states emissions in kilograms instead of tonnes; the engineer converts every project's emissions to kilograms but leaves the emissions reference at 200, meant as tonnes. What happens to emissions in the value?

options.text: Its pull stays the same, since a normalized score does not depend on units
options.says: The units cancel only when the reference is restated with the measure; here it was not.

options.text: Its pull drops a thousandfold, since the reference alone stayed in tonnes
options.says: The measures grew a thousandfold over the same reference, so the scores grow, not shrink.

options.text: Its pull grows a thousandfold, since the measures alone moved to kilograms
options.says: Right: m is now 1,000 times larger and R is not, so every emissions score is 1,000 times too big.

options.text: The solver refuses the model, since a measure and its reference disagree in unit
options.says: Nothing checks units; every number still looks reasonable, which is why a test must restate them.

origin.section: A Normalized Score Divides by a Reference, So the Units Cancel

questions.stem: Scores are min-max scaled, so the worst candidate on each measure scores 0 and the best scores 1. The board compares a plan of three projects with a plan of one by their total score. What does the scaling do to that comparison?

options.text: It deducts the worst candidate's benefit per project, which handicaps the larger plan
options.says: Right: each project is scored on its excess over the worst, so each one added pays that deduction again.

options.text: It deducts the worst candidate's benefit per plan, which treats both plans alike
options.says: The deduction is inside every project's score, so it is paid once for each project in the sum.

options.text: It adds the worst candidate's benefit per project, which favors the larger plan
options.says: Min-max subtracts the worst candidate's level; it adds nothing.

options.text: It changes no comparison, since min-max scaling cancels units as a ratio does
options.says: It does cancel units, but it also moves zero away from no benefit, which matters for sums.

origin.section: Zero Must Mean No Benefit When Scores Are Added Across Projects

questions.stem: Each measure's reference is set to the best candidate's benefit in it. A project that leads two of the measures is withdrawn, and the rest are scored again. What happens to the projects that stay?

options.text: Their scores stay put, since each score uses only that project's own benefits
options.says: That holds for fixed references; here the references themselves shrink.

options.text: Their scores in those two measures shrink, since those references grow
options.says: The best remaining benefit is smaller than the withdrawn leader's, so the references shrink.

options.text: Their scores all shrink by one common factor, so their order cannot move
options.says: Only two measures change, so the scores do not move by one common factor and the order can change.

options.text: Their scores in those two measures grow, and their order can then move
options.says: Right: smaller references raise those measures' pull, as GridCap small's top five showed.

origin.section: The Reference Is Fixed Before the Candidates Are Scored
